newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Elephants to dominate endangered species meeting.
newsitem.headline: Elephants to dominate endangered species meeting.

text.p: A proposal to resume trade in ivory from the African elephant is expected to be the dominant issue at a world conference on endangered species that starts in Zimbabwe on Monday.

The 10-day Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) meeting has been preceeded by a spirited debate. CITES officials say the delegates and the public will also be watching decisions on whales.

"For us, all the issues on our agenda are important but for many people the conference has become a conference on elephants alone," CITES Secretary-General Izgrev Topkov said last Wednesday when he arrived in the Zimbabwean capital to prepare for the meeting.
"We have 115 agenda items. We have 89 tags for species and 75 proposals. The media should not only report on elephants," he complained.

The debate on elephants has been sparked by a proposal from three elephant-rich southern African states -- Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe -- for CITES to lift a seven-year-old world ban in ivory trade and to allow "limited but strictly supervised trade".

They and their supporters, notably Japan, argue that ivory trade has never threatened the three countries' elephant herds, saying they were rising even before the 1989 ban, and now at around 150,000, are over twice the land's carrying capacity.
The southern African states say since they have to stabilise their elephant populations, there is no sound reason not to earn revenue by selling culled ivory.
But many "green" organisations and countries, including the United States and France, oppose the proposal, saying it will be difficult to manage and will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.
CITES officials expect the issue to be heavily contested before a vote is taken in the 138-member organisation towards the end of the conference.

Amsterdam-based environment group Green Peace says pro-trade lobbyists are seeking a secret ballot to win support from Western governments who may be afraid to openly take positions that may anger their domestic constituencies.
"Since democratic governments are accountable to the public for their policies, their votes should be public too," it said in a statement.
Some 3,000 delegates and observers are scheduled to attend the meeting, which CITES officials said could also see intense debate on a proposal by Japan and Norway to open up whale-hunting.

The conference will also debate ways to preserve the Indian tiger, the black rhino, the sturgeon fish and the Cuban sea turtle, all said by many environment watchdogs to be threatened by poachers feeding a thriving illegal industry. CITES estimates illegal global trade in endangered species at up to $10 billion a year.
